title: BARRINGTON, George. AN ACCOUNT OF A VOYAGE TO NEW SOUTH WALES [together with] THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including
description: BARRINGTON, George. AN ACCOUNT OF A VOYAGE TO NEW SOUTH WALES [together with] THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including Botany Bay, Port Jackson, Pamaratta [sic], Sydney, and all its Dependancies from the Original Discovery of the Island: with the Customs and Manners of the Natives; and an Account of the English Colony, from its Foundation, to the Present Time. Two volumes, octavo, handcoloured engraved vignette titles to each volume, portrait and handcoloured frontispiece to the Voyage and handcoloured frontispiece to the History, folding handcoloured map, 22 handcoloured plates, and full-page woodcut in-text, without List of Plates, one plate just shaved, one page number punched, uniformly bound in later half calf and marbled boards, Sydney Spence’s copy with his stamp. London, Printed for M. Jones, 1803 - 1802. First editions: an attractive set of this important early account of New South Wales, the first book on the colony with coloured views. Originally issued in parts and then as cased volumes for at least half a dozen years, there are many variants of the book, most notable in the preliminaries. The present copy is a typical copy, complete as issued. This copy of the History has the half-title and also the rarely encountered leaf: “The Publisher to the Reader”. In common with other sets, some of the plates published with the 1803 Voyage are here bound, more appropriately, in the History volume. See Ferguson, 367 (Voyage), and Ferguson, 345 (History), although the uncommon title misspelling of “Pamaratta” and the “The Publisher to the Reader” leaf are not noted by him nor in the 1986 Addenda. Estimate $2000/3000

title: BRETON, William Henry.
description: BRETON, William Henry. EXCURSIONS IN NEW SOUTH WALES, Western Australia, and Van Diemen’s Land, in the years 1830, 1831, 1832, and 1833. Octavo, aquatint frontispiece foxed and with early sealed tear, in early half morocco and marbled boards by Pownceby of Melbourne. London, Richard Bentley, 1833. First edition. Ferguson, 1631 (miscollated). Estimate $200/300

title: CLARK, John Heaviside.
description: CLARK, John Heaviside. FIELD SPORTS, &c. &c. OF THE NATIVE INHABITANTS OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Quarto, with ten fine handcoloured aquatint plates, some marking and toning, in handsome modern olive straight grain morocco, the boards within gilt Greek key pattern border, spine lettered in Regency style, marbled endpapers. London, Edward Orme, 1813. First edition: an early state of this important Australian plate book; in those instances where a watermark is present it is dated 1810 or 1811, as in the earliest issues. The first published book on the Australian Aborigines, this important New South Wales supplement of ten handcoloured aquatint plates of Australian Aboriginal scenes with descriptive text was issued both separately and with the large main work – Orme’s Foreign Field Sports, Fisheries, Sporting Anecdotes, &c. &c., one of the most notable books from the golden age of the handcoloured illustrated book. The plates here represent in vivid style and delicate detail various aspects of Aboriginal life in the bush. Some of the plates show hunting scenes such as kangaroo hunting, fishing, bird hunting, and smoking out possums. Other plates represent aspects of tribal life such as a corroboree, trial by spear, a war party, and a night scene in a camp. The plates are justly celebrated and are without question the most attractive and sympathetic of the early European depictions of the Aboriginal inhabitants. Ferguson, 551; Wantrup, 213a. Estimate $2000/3000

title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY in New South Wales, from its first Settlement in January 1788, to Augus
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY in New South Wales, from its first Settlement in January 1788, to August 1801; With Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants... Quarto, with a map and folding chart, 24 engraved plates (three handcoloured), eight engravings in the text (two handcoloured), a number of plates without imprints as often, stamp erased from title page, contemporary half calf and marbled boards, rebacked, head of spine detached, corners wearing. London, T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1804. Second edition, abridged by Maria Collins, with new information available to the end of 1803. This is the preferred issue with handcoloured natural history plates: another issue has uncoloured plates. With the text mispaginated as in all copies – page numerals 313-322 are used twice, while numerals 289-298 are not used. Ferguson, 390; Wantrup 21 (miscounting preliminaries). Estimate $1200/1800

title: COOK, Captain James. CAPTAIN COOK’S THREE VOYAGES TO THE PACIFIC OCEAN... faithfully abridged from the quarto editions.
description: COOK, Captain James. CAPTAIN COOK’S THREE VOYAGES TO THE PACIFIC OCEAN... faithfully abridged from the quarto editions. containing a particular relation of all the interesting transactions during the several voyages. to which is prefixed, the life of Captain Cook. Two volumes, duodecimo, with seven (of eight) engraved plates, modern calf in contemporary style, somewhat browned as often with American books of the period, general soiling and use, owner’s stamp on the title-page of the first volume and in other places, earlier ownership marks on the titles, with the bookplate of Donald H. Graham. Boston, Manning and Loring for Thomas & Andrews and D. West, 1797. The very scarce first American edition of Cook’s collected voyages. The first and second voyages are covered in the first volume, with the third voyage in the second volume. The eight copper plates include a reduced version of one of the Northwest Coast plates, making this the first view of the Northwest Coast published in the United States, and a plate depicting the death of Cook. All eighteenth-century American editions of Cook are rare. Beddie, 58; Forbes, 270; Sabin, 20366. Estimate $1000/1500

title: COOK, James. CAPTAIN COOK’S VOYAGES ROUND THE WORLD, Containing The Whole of his Discoveries [engraved title].
description: COOK, James. CAPTAIN COOK’S VOYAGES ROUND THE WORLD, Containing The Whole of his Discoveries [engraved title]. Quarto, frontispiece, additional engraved title, engraved plates and vignettes, several plates stregnthened at short marginal tears, contemporary calf, well rebacked retaining the original spine and label. London, J. Robins & Co., Albion Press, 1822. A very scarce large format collected edition of Cook in one volume, with text printed in double column. Estimate $500/800

title: COOK. KIPPIS, Andrew. THE LIFE OF CAPTAIN JAMES COOK. Octavo, early tree calf, later rebacked and recornered.
description: COOK. KIPPIS, Andrew. THE LIFE OF CAPTAIN JAMES COOK. Octavo, early tree calf, later rebacked and recornered. Dublin, H. Chamberlaine, W. Colles (and others), 1788. The rare Dublin edition of Kippis’s great biography of Cook, the first biography of the explorer. This Dublin edition was published immediately after the London edition and, as is often the case with the Dublin piracies, it is much rarer than the original. Kippis had access to Admiralty sources as well as documents belonging to Joseph Banks, and attempted a full account of Cook’s public life. He includes a long account of Cook’s death from Samwell’s rare pamphlet (which Kippis had helped to be published): “I procured its publication, that, if any objections should be made to it, I might be able to notice them in my own work. As the narrative hath continued for more than two years unimpeached and uncontradicted, I esteem myself fully authorised to insert it in this place, as containing the most complete and authentic account of the melancholy catastrophe, which, at Owhyee, befell our illustrious navigator and Commander...”. Beddie, 34 (in error, corrected by Forbes); Forbes, 152; Hill 2, 936, Kroepelien, 648. Estimate $1000/2000 Lot 8

title: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor.
description: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor. NEW SOUTH WALES. PAPERS EXPLANATORY OF THE CHARGES brought against Lieut. Gen. Darling, by William Charles Wentworth, Esq. Foolscap folio, without the terminal endorsement leaf (blank apart from docket title on verso); bound in modern quarter calf. London, Ordered, by The House of Commons, to be Printed, 1 July 1830. Following the agitation of opposition Members of Parliament, the Colonial Secretary published these dispatches from New South Wales. The tabling of these papers was a thoroughly dishonest representation of the Wentworth – Darling affair, anticipating, without ambiguity, the way the government would handle the whole matter. Darling’s dispatches relating to Wentworth’s attempted impeachment of him with all the various attachments and enclosures were printed here “exclusive of a Letter, also therein enclosed, addressed by Mr. William Charles Wentworth to the Right Honourable Sir George Murray…”. In other words, Darling’s defence against Wentworth’s charges, the Executive Council’s detailed critical response to Wentworth’s letter of impeachment, and other supporting documents were laid upon the table and printed but not the very case for impeachment that formed the crux of the entire affair! Once this deceptive conduct was revealed by Robison and his allies in the famous pamphlet by “Miles”, the Colonial Office was forced to reveal the entire text of the Wentworth impeachment and it was published in the parliamentary papers in 1832 as paper 620 of that year. Ferguson, 1355. Estimate $1000/2000

title: DARLING. WENTWORTH, William Charles.
description: DARLING. WENTWORTH, William Charles. NEW SOUTH WALES: JOSEPH SUDDS. Return to an Address of The Honourable the House of Commons, dated 5 July 1832; – for, A Return of all the Letters addressed by the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for the Colonies, in reply to Governor Darling’s Despatches, relative to the Punishment and Death of Private Joseph Sudds, late of His Majesty’s 57th Regiment, dated 4th & l2th December 1826, and 20th April and 28th May 1829; – Also, for the portions of Mr. Wentworth’s Letter of Impeachment which have been omitted in the Returns laid upon the Table of The House on lst July 1830. Foolscap folio, with the terminal endorsement leaf (bearing small stamp of Incorporated Law Society), bound in modern quarter calf. [London], Ordered, by The House of Commons, to be Printed, 20 July 1832. Rare: the somewhat reluctant printing in the parliamentary papers of Wentworth’s letter to Sir George Murray impeaching Darling’s conduct in the case of Sudds and Thompson. This order of the House of Commons followed the deceitful publication in 1830 of Papers Explanatory of the Charges brought against Lieut. Gen. Darling, by William Charles Wentworth, Esq., in which virtually every relevant document was published except Wentworth’s crucial letter of impeachment. Even now, under pressure from opposition Members of Parliament and the press, the government found it difficult not to be coy – titling this paper under the main heading “Joseph Sudds” and burying the reference to Wentworth’s letter under an eight-line description of a relatively trivial one-and-a-half-page dispatch printed on the first two pages of the present paper. A process that strikes one as almost ludicrously disingenuous. Wentworth’s letter to Murray occupies pages 2 to 54 of this 56-page paper: this is the first and only complete publication of the Wentworth letter apart from the unpublished Sydney printing. Ferguson, 1551. Estimate $2000/4000

title: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor.
description: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor. REPORT FROM SELECT COMMITTEE on the Conduct of General Darling, while Governor of New South Wales. With the Minutes of Evidence, and Appendix. Foolscap folio, careful restoration to small scratch on wrapper and first few leaves, uncut, with the original printed blue paper wrappers in modern blue half morocco. [London], House of Commons, 1 September 1835. Very scarce: “an extremely important source of information with reference to this famous case” (Ferguson). The Report was viewed, not without justice, as a whitewash of Darling by his political cronies. Ferguson, 1960. Estimate $300/500 Lot 9

title: FIELD, Barron. GEOGRAPHICAL MEMOIRS ON NEW SOUTH WALES; by various hands: Containing an account of the Surveyor General’
description: FIELD, Barron. GEOGRAPHICAL MEMOIRS ON NEW SOUTH WALES; by various hands: Containing an account of the Surveyor General’s late expedition to two new ports; the discovery of Moreton Bay River, with the adventures for seven months there of two shipwrecked men; a route from Bathurst to Liverpool Plains; Together with other papers on the Aborigines, the geology, the botany, the timber, the astronomy, and the meteorology of New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land. Edited by Barron Field, Esq. F.L.S. Late Judge of the Supreme Court of New South Wales and its Dependencies. Octavo, with aquatint frontispiece (foxed and offset to title), the two botanical plates stained at one corner and foxed, four folding maps, an uncut copy in later half morocco, top edge gilt. London, John Murray, 1825. First edition. Of high exploration interest, Field’s Geographical Memoirs includes, among many other papers, an account of Allan Cunningham’s important exploration to the Liverpool Plains, Currie’s excursion to the southward of Lake George, the journal of Barron Field’s trip across the Blue Mountains, and, perhaps most importantly, two accounts of Oxley’s 1823 Moreton Bay expedition. Ferguson, 1009; Perry and Prescott, 1825.02-05 (maps); Wantrup, 108. Estimate $1200/1800

title: FIELD, Barron. AN ANALYSIS OF BLACKSTONE’S COMMENTARIES on the Laws of England, in a series of questions, to which the s
description: FIELD, Barron. AN ANALYSIS OF BLACKSTONE’S COMMENTARIES on the Laws of England, in a series of questions, to which the student is to frame his own answers, by reading that work. Octavo, early owner’s signature, uncut and partly unopened, original boards with paper label, the spine chipped. London, Cadell and Davies, 1811. Rare: first edition of an early legal work by Field before his appointment to the bench in New South Wales. Not in Ferguson nor the 1986 Addenda. Estimate $600/800

title: FORSTER, Johann Reinhold.
description: FORSTER, Johann Reinhold. OBSERVATIONS MADE DURING A VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD on Physical Geography, Natural History and Ethic Philosophy. Beddie, 1261; Holmes, 29; Renard, 550; Rosove, 140.A1; Spence, 467. Estimate $400/600

title: GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND, Parliament.
description: GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND, Parliament. REPORT FROM THE SELECT COMMITTEE ON SECONDARY PUNISHMENTS. Together with the Minutes of Evidence, an Appendix of Papers, and an Index [together with] REPORT FROM THE SELECT COMMITTEE on Secondary Punishments… 1832. Two volumes in one, foolscap folio, later half calf, spine fading and with one spot. London, House of Commons, 1831 and 1832. Amongst the witnesses in 1831 are James Busby, J. H. Capper, and E.G. Wakefield. Ferguson, 1432. Of the scarce 1832 Report, Ferguson says: “A very important report. Includes evidence by Mrs. Fry, John Stephens, Alan Cunningham, James Busby, and A.B. (a discharged convict)”. Ferguson, 1543. + CONVICTS. Commitments, Trials, Convictions &c. Returns in compliance with the Act… Foolscap folio, inked pagination from a previous binding, modern wrappers with printed label. (London, Ordered, by the House of Commons, to be printed, 24 February 1817.) Tables of trials and sentencing. With, loosely inserted, a separate single leaf printing “A Statement of the Nature of the Crimes of which the persons were convicted, who had sentence of Death passed upon them, and of the number who were executed… Ordered by the House of Commons to be printed, 22 March 1819”. Estimate $500/800

title: HOWARD, John. THE STATE OF THE PRISONS in England and Wales, With Preliminary Observations, and an account of some Forei
description: HOWARD, John. THE STATE OF THE PRISONS in England and Wales, With Preliminary Observations, and an account of some Foreign Prisons and Hospitals. Octavo, eleven folding engraved plates, a fine uncut copy in original papered boards, housed in quarter morocco book form box. Warrington, T. Cadell and M. Conant, 1780. Second edition. Estimate $300/500

title: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL OF THE TRANSACTIONS AT PORT JACKSON AND NORFOLK ISLAND, with discoveries which have
description: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL OF THE TRANSACTIONS AT PORT JACKSON AND NORFOLK ISLAND, with discoveries which have been made in New South Wales and in the Southern Ocean, since the publication of Phillip’s Voyage… Quarto, frontispiece, engraved title-page (complete with date), with small repaired excision, plates and folding maps (few repairs), handsome period style half calf and marbled boards, spine gilt. London, John Stockdale, 1793. First edition: a finely-bound copy (with wide margins) of this ‘official’ First Fleet narrative, written by the second governor, which continues Phillip’s 1789 Voyage as the official account of the first years of settlement at Sydney. Hunter gives an excellent account of many activities, particularly exploration and the settlement at Norfolk Island (based on Philip Gidley King’s papers), which are treated more cursorily by the other First Fleet chroniclers. The engraved plates and maps, many of the latter from original cartography by Hunter, Dawes, and Bradley, are very fine. Among other plates – most notably William Blake’s engraving of an Aboriginal family after a drawing by Philip Gidley King – is the first published view of the First Fleet settlement at Sydney Cove, engraved by Edward Dayes after a drawing by Hunter. The view shows the settlement at Sydney Cove at the very earliest stage of its development. Davidson, pp. 87-9 (“essential”); Ferguson, 152; Hill 2, 857; McCormick, First Views, plate 7ff; Wantrup, 13. Estimate $3000/5000

title: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL OF THE TRANSACTIONS AT PORT JACKSON AND NORFOLK ISLAND, with discoveries which have
description: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL OF THE TRANSACTIONS AT PORT JACKSON AND NORFOLK ISLAND, with discoveries which have been made in New South Wales and in the Southern Ocean, since the publication of Phillip’s Voyage… Quarto, with an engraved title-page (complete with date), portrait frontispiece, eleven plates, and four folding maps, in a handsome Bayntun-Riviere binding of marbled boards and quarter tan crushed morocco, the spine with raised bands, gilt. London, John Stockdale, 1793. First edition: a handsome large copy of this ‘official’ First Fleet narrative. Stockdale’s edition of Governor Hunter’s journal is a continuation of the 1789 edition of Governor Phillip’s voyage. Ferguson, 152; McCormick, First Views, plate 7ff; Wantrup, 13. Estimate $3000/5000

title: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY OF THE INTERTROPICAL AND WESTERN COASTS OF AUSTRALIA, performed between the
description: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY OF THE INTERTROPICAL AND WESTERN COASTS OF AUSTRALIA, performed between the years 1818 and 1822. Two volumes, octavo, plates and maps, folding map, the plates and maps a little offset and foxed as usual, errata leaf for both volumes in volume two (as issued), bound without half-titles in contemporary polished calf, marbled edges and endpapers, top of the spines a little worn, the copy of Sir Charles Edward Stirling with armorial bookplate, in modern folding book box with the bookplate of Geoffrey Cains. London, John Murray, 1826. First edition: the extremely rare first issue with title-pages dated 1826. Admiral Phillip Parker King, Australian-born son of the third governor, Philip Gidley King, became the Navy’s leading hydrographer. Despatched by the Admiralty and the Colonial Office to complete Flinders’s interrupted survey and firmly to establish Great Britain’s claim to the north coast, King charted the greater part of the west, north and north-east coasts and also carried out important surveys in the area of the Barrier Reef. His hydrographical work is still the basis of many of the modern charts for the areas he surveyed. First published in April 1826, the first issue of this classic Australian voyage is “a notorious rarity” (Wantrup). Late in 1826 or early in 1827 the publisher, John Murray, had the original title-page dated 1826 excised and replaced with a cancel title-page dated 1827. Known to Ferguson in only one copy and to Davidson in less than a handful, about a dozen are now recorded. It is one of the most conspicuous rarities in Australian collecting. Davidson, pp. 127-8; Ferguson, 1084; Wantrup, 84a and see also pp. 161-3. Estimate $15,000/20,000

title: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY of the intertropical and western coasts of Australia, performed between the
description: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY of the intertropical and western coasts of Australia, performed between the years 1818 and 1822. Two volumes, octavo, plates and maps, folding map, errata slip in the first volume, bound without half-titles in half calf and marbled boards of the period, joints cracking, with the bookplates of John Warren Bakewell, and Edward Charles Stirling. London, John Murray, 1827. First edition: the standard issue with title-pages dated 1827. Ferguson, 1084; Wantrup, 84b. Estimate $2000/3000

title: LANG, John Dunmore. ACCOUNT OF THE STEPS TAKEN in England, with a view to the establishment of an Academical Institution
description: LANG, John Dunmore. ACCOUNT OF THE STEPS TAKEN in England, with a view to the establishment of an Academical Institution, or College, in New South Wales; and to demonstrate the practicability of effecting an extensive emigration of the Industrious classes Octavo, foxing, modern calf backed boards. Sydney, Stephens and Stokes, 1831. Uncommon. Ferguson, 1448. Estimate $400/600 Lot 18

title: LYCETT, Joseph. VIEWS IN AUSTRALIA OR NEW SOUTH WALES, & VAN DIEMEN’S LAND DELINEATED, IN FIFTY VIEWS, with descriptive
description: LYCETT, Joseph. VIEWS IN AUSTRALIA OR NEW SOUTH WALES, & VAN DIEMEN’S LAND DELINEATED, IN FIFTY VIEWS, with descriptive Letter Press, Dedicated by Permission, to The Right Honble. Earl Bathurst, &c. &c. &c. By J. Lycett, Artist to Major General Macquarie, late Governor of those Colonies. Oblong folio, handcoloured lithographed title and 48 handcoloured aquatint views after drawings by Joseph Lycett (three plates with oxidised spotting), with descriptive text (some short splits at margin neatly sealed), and two folding maps, in superb nineteenth-century polished calf by Rivière, housed in a matching felt-lined calf box by Aquarius. London, J. Souter, 1825. First edition of the finest Australian topographical plate book of the pre-gold rush era and the outstanding artistic monument to the age of Macquarie. Joseph Lycett, a forger and professional painter of portraits and miniatures, arrived in New South Wales in 1814 on the same ship that brought James Wallis to the colony. A little over twelve months after his arrival he was again convicted of forgery and sentenced to a term in Newcastle, the place of punishment for convicts who committed further crimes in the colony. Here he came again into contact with James Wallis, who arrived to take command of the penal settlement about a year after Lycett had been sent there. Lycett’s good work in designing the new church in Newcastle, his painted altar-piece and the other drawings and paintings he made for Wallis earned him a conditional pardon in 1819. After 1819 Lycett appears to have travelled and painted extensively in New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land. Macquarie was clearly impressed by his skill and employed him somewhat in the capacity of unofficial government artist, finally granting him an absolute pardon in 1821. The pardon enabled him to return to England in 1823 and finish the book of views he had been planning. The 48 views in this work offer a comprehensive record of Macquarie’s Australia, from the settled areas to the frontier. In particular, Lycett’s depiction of various private mansions and country seats – demonstrating the progress of wealth and civilisation in the colonies – is an incomparable record of early colonial architecture and garden design. In its fine Rivière binding, this is the most attractive copy of this seminal book that we have handled in many years. Abbey, 570; Ferguson, 1031; Wantrup, 218b. Estimate $40,000/60,000 THIS IS THE BLANK REVERSE OF THE FOLDING PLATE Please fold out Lot 21 Lycett’s Views in a fine early Rivière binding

title: MACARTHUR, James. NEW SOUTH WALES; ITS PRESENT STATE AND FUTURE PROSPECTS: being a Statement, with Documentary Evidence,
description: MACARTHUR, James. NEW SOUTH WALES; ITS PRESENT STATE AND FUTURE PROSPECTS: being a Statement, with Documentary Evidence, submitted in support of Petitions to His Majesty and Parliament. Octavo, with handcoloured folding map trimmed at foot, with half-title, several gatherings with pale staining, in worn but sound original green moiré cloth. London, D. Walther, 1837. First edition: an excellent presentation copy of this important political statement prepared by James Macarthur and edited anonymously for him by noted British librarian Edward Edwards, is a comprehensive and well-documented account of the colony from the social, political and economic point of view. The present copy was presented by James Macarthur, inscribed on the title-page to “Admiral Hawker from his sincere friend J. McA. London, 20th Novr. 1837”. Ferguson, 2304. Estimate $500/700

title: MOLESWORTH, Sir William (Chairman).
description: MOLESWORTH, Sir William (Chairman). REPORT FROM THE SELECT COMMITTEE ON TRANSPORTATION Together with the Minutes of Evidence, Appendix, and Index. Foolscap folio, with errata slip, stamp on title and final leaf, a clean copy in modern cloth with paper spine label. London, Ordered by the House of Commons to be Printed, 3 August 1838. An important and highly influential report, under the Chairmanship of Sir William Molesworth; with evidence from (inter alia) Rev. William Ullathorne, Sir Edward Parry, and Major Thomas Mitchell. Ferguson notes that startling particulars of the conditions on Norfolk Island are given. Ferguson, 2500. Estimate $300/500

title: O’HARA, James. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Second Edition.
description: O’HARA, James. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Second Edition. Octavo, 1823 owner’s name on title, with the half-title, a good copy in later half calf and marbled boards, the Tristan Buesst copy with bookplate. London, Printed for J. Hatchard, 1818. This was the first general history of New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land that was not merely a compilation, or plagiarism, of earlier first-hand accounts. O’Hara’s book is of particular note for its record of the otherwise virtually unobtainable reports of the explorations of George William Evans, whose discoveries proved to be of greater consequence than those of his predecessors and contemporaries. First published anonymously the year before by O’Hara himself, this is the second Hatchard issue of the original sheets, the third issue overall. All early issues are very scarce. “The first true history of the colony... O’Hara provides the best picture of the first half of Macquarie’s rule, the Golden Age, that we have between two covers” (Wantrup). Ferguson, 725; Wantrup, 40 (note) and p. 110. Estimate $700/900

title: OGLE, Nathaniel. THE COLONY OF WESTERN AUSTRALIA: a Manual for Emigrants to that Settlement or its Dependencies: Compris
description: OGLE, Nathaniel. THE COLONY OF WESTERN AUSTRALIA: a Manual for Emigrants to that Settlement or its Dependencies: Comprising its Discovery, Settlement, Aborigines, Land-Regulations, Principles of Colonial Emigration; Statistical, Financial, and Agricultural Reports; also Instructions and Hints to Settlers, Directions for the Anchorages, &c.; with the most correct Map extant… With an Appendix, containing the Government Commission, Land-Regulations, a List of the Names of the Proprietors, their Original Grants and Number of Acres, Tenures, Conditions, Transfers, &c. Taken from Official Documents. Octavo, with four folding tables, four etched plates (two folding), and large folding handcoloured Arrowsmith map (530 x 610 mm) in rear endpocket, uncut, in fine recent half calf and marbled boards, spine gilt and with crimson labels. London, James Fraser, 1839. First edition of a highly important work on the new colony of Western Australia. Ferguson, 2819. Estimate $2000/4000

title: OXLEY, John. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF NEW SOUTH WALES, undertaken by order of the British Govern
description: OXLEY, John. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF NEW SOUTH WALES, undertaken by order of the British Government in the Years 1817-18. By John Oxley, Surveyor General of the Territory and Lieutenant of the Royal Navy. With Maps and Views of the Interior, or newly discovered country. Quarto, with the sectional title, one folding engraved plate, five aquatint plates (two handcoloured), three folding charts, and two folding tables, a signed Morrell binding of half morocco, all edges gilt. London, John Murray, 1820. First edition of the foundation work of Australian inland exploration and the first detailed description of the interior of New South Wales to be published. Surveyor-General John Oxley’s narrative of his two major expeditions, issued in an edition of only 500 copies, includes a fine hand-coloured aquatint portrait of an Aboriginal chief by John William Lewin, as well as an evocative series of aquatint landscape views drawn by Major James Taylor from sketches by George William Evans. Ferguson, 796; Wantrup, 107. Estimate $5000/7000

title: PALMER, Thomas Fyshe. A NARRATIVE OF THE SUFFERINGS OF T.F. PALMER, AND W. SKIRVING, during a voyage to New South Wales,
description: PALMER, Thomas Fyshe. A NARRATIVE OF THE SUFFERINGS OF T.F. PALMER, AND W. SKIRVING, during a voyage to New South Wales, 1794, on board the Surprise transport... Octavo, speckled half calf by Sangorski, top edge gilt, others uncut, Coles copy with bookplate. Cambridge, printed by Benjamin Flower, for J. Deighton and others, 1797. Rare: the most interesting and detailed of the very few published accounts by a transportee, recording his appalling experiences on board a convict transport. Palmer and Skirving were not convicted felons but gentlemen and political exiles. Victimised by the captain of the Surprize, Palmer and Skirving made successful representations to the Governor on their arrival and were largely vindicated. Palmer was convicted of sedition in 1793 after he arranged for the printing and distribution of an address on parliamentary reform. “He sailed for New South Wales in April 1794 in the transport Surprize, which also carried his fellow Scottish Martyrs, Thomas Muir, William Skirving and Maurice Margarot. When in the tropics, Captain Campbell, master of the Surprize, acting on ill-founded charges of incitement to mutiny, confined Palmer and Skirving under conditions of extreme hardship, which were the subject of complaints laid before Lieutenant-Governor Francis Grose on their arrival at Sydney on 25 October. A narrative describing his sufferings was taken back to England by Surgeon John White and published in 1797 ... Palmer was probably the most cultured of those who came to New South Wales in the early years of settlement. Humane in sentiment and advanced in political opinion, he gained the friendship of the more liberal minded surgeons, White and Bass; but his radical views on politics and religion were looked at with suspicion in a penal colony and aroused the animosity of certain officers … and of Governor Hunter” (ADB). In addition to his account of the voyage, Palmer includes in this pamphlet much relating to the earliest years of the colony and this second edition has an important addition, “A Letter from Messrs. Muir, Palmer, and Skirving, to Governor Hunter” dated 14 October 1795, which comprises the final six pages. This is the second of two Cambridge editions of the same year; there was also a London edition: all are rare. Ferguson, 255. Estimate $2000/4000

title: PHILLIP, Arthur. EXTRACTS OF LETTERS FROM ARTHUR PHILLIP, ESQ. Governor of New South Wales, to Lord Sydney; to which is

Governor of New South Wales, to Lord Sydney; to which is annexed a description of Norfolk Island, by Philip Gidley King, Esq. and An Account of Expences incurred in transporting Convicts to New South Wales. With sixty-five plates of nondescript animals, birds, lizards, serpents… Quarto, 65 engraved plates, a little pale foxing, generally clean, in contemporary tree calf, joints cracked, with the engraved bookplates of Sir Drummond Smith, and Edward Charles Stirling. John White was the chief surgeon on the First Fleet and Surgeon-general to the settlement, whose most remarkable, if still little recognised, achievement was the minuscule mortality rates among the convicts on the long voyage from England to New South Wales, in what is still one of the largest mass movements of humanity ever undertaken. He continued to overcome severe medical problems in the first settlement, working in atrocious conditions, and even became a pioneer of the use of native Australian plants as medicine. His journal commences with the sailing of the First Fleet, including an account of the voyage from England. His personal chronicle of the first ten months of settlement includes “many circumstances omitted by Governor Arthur Phillip and others” (Hill). title: WHITEHEAD, Isaac (attributed).
description: WHITEHEAD, Isaac (attributed). CROSSING THE BLUE MOUNTAINS (titled on the stretcher and the frame) Oil on canvas, 855 x 1130 mm, in original gilt frame. A little old scuffing to the edges where the canvas meets the frame, otherwise in very good state. [Melbourne, 1860s-1870s] A fine painting in the historical and topographical genre celebrating the history and extraordinarily rapid development of the Australian colonies that had a particular vogue in Australia in the decades following the gold rush. The almost triumphant spirit of those years felt the need of an epic past, a need that was satisfied in part by the historical genre paintings supplied by colonial artists throughout the 1860s and 1870s and in literature by historical novelists such as Marcus Clarke (lot 81) and Charles de Boos (lot 82). The successful construction of the road across the Blue Mountains by William Cox in 1814-1815, following in the wake of Blaxland, Wentworth, and Lawson, was arguably the greatest work of civil engineering undertaken in the first fifty years of European settlement and a particularly apt subject for epic historical painting. Isaac Whitehead was a prolific painter of mainly landscape views who, although based in Melbourne, exhibited widely in Victoria, New Zealand, and New South Wales, and did so with great public and critical success. His artistic output in the two decades he spent in Australia and in New Zealand (as a traveller) before his death in 1881 was prodigious, given his parallel career as a highly regarded art and mirror framer. His high reputation as an artist was forgotten in the 1890s, when the painters of the Heidelberg School became the focus of critical attention. His paintings are represented in major Australian collections. See further the long article on him in Joan Kerr (ed.) Dictionary of Australian Artists… to 1870. title: CLACY, Ellen, née Sturmer.
description: CLACY, Ellen, née Sturmer. A LADY’S VISIT TO THE GOLD DIGGINGS OF AUSTRALIA, IN 1852-53. Written on the Spot by Mrs. Charles Clacy. Duodecimo, engraved frontispiece, sewing loosening, original blindstamped cloth (fading and a bit worn). London, Hurst and Blackett, 1853. First edition of one of the classics of gold rush literature, the most vivid account of daily life on the goldfields ever published, and the first eye-witness account of the diggings written by a woman (and for several years the only one). It was “written on the spot” at the Victorian diggings, where Ellen Sturmer kept house for her brother and a small party as they moved from one field to another. This genteel young daughter of a clergyman, against all convention, accompanied her brother on a wild, daring escapade. The commission, chaired skilfully by William Westgarth, refused to follow Hotham’s instruction that they were not to investigate the causes of Eureka, and their “statesmanlike report” recommended a general amnesty as well as equitable arrangements for miner’s rights and enfranchisement. description: LEICHHARDT, Friedrich Wilhelm Ludwig. title: STRZELECKI, Count Paul Edmond de.
description: STRZELECKI, Count Paul Edmond de. PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION OF NEW SOUTH WALES AND VAN DIEMEN’S LAND. Accompanied by a Geological Map, Sections, and Diagrams, and Figures of the organic remains. Octavo, with handcoloured folding map, three tinted lithographs, 19 plain plates (one folding), some plates a little foxed, uncut in the original cloth, front board with splash marks. London, Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, 1845. First edition: presentation copy inscribed “A token of remembrance from the Author” at the head of the title. The scientific narrative of Strzelecki’s 7000-mile excursion on foot with James Macarthur and a small party through New South Wales, across the Australian Alps into Gippsland, and then into Van Diemen’s Land. This book, for which Strzelecki received the Founder’s medal of the Royal Geographical Society in London, was the first extensive scientific survey of any part of Australia and laid the foundation of Australian palaeontology. The geological map, bound here as frontispiece, was one of the earliest and most ambitious attempts to prepare a geological map of any part of the continent. Ferguson overlooks the view of “Ben Nevis and Ben Lomond” (at p. 164) and the portrait of “Jemmy” (at p. 333). Ferguson, 4168 (omitting two plates); Forbes, 1568; Richards, 117. Estimate $800/1200

title: TERRY, Frederick C. LANDSCAPE SCENERY, Illustrating Sydney, Paramatta, Richmond, Maitland, Windsor, and Port Jackson, New South Wales.
description: TERRY, Frederick C. LANDSCAPE SCENERY, Illustrating Sydney, Paramatta, Richmond, Maitland, Windsor, and Port Jackson, New South Wales. Oblong quarto, with title and 38 engraved plates by F.C. Terry, one caption altered in ink and with pencilled locations added to many other captions, original ornately gilt-decorated blue morocco-grain cloth, “Australian Keepsake 1855” in gilt on the front board, all edges gilt, neatly rebacked with original spine. Sydney and Melbourne, Sands and Kenny, 1855 (but December, 1854). First edition of Terry’s wellknown series of delicate vignette views of Sydney scenes. This is the first issue, with the errata slip dated December 23, 1854, that is present only in the earliest copies issued. John Sands, an enterprising English emigrant, was the first to recognise the potential market for popular books of Australian views. His first venture in the field was in 1854 when he commissioned a series of landscape views of Sydney and the surrounding districts from Frederick Terry and had them engraved in England for publication and sale in Australia. In December 1854 Sands was advertising the Australian Keepsake for sale at twenty-five shillings. His next venture was to commission S.T. Gill to prepare a series of views of Victoria: Victoria Illustrated was issued in December 1856, with a second series in 1862. For some unknown reason Sands had 39 plates prepared but included only 38 of these in the published copies (see Wantrup, loc.cit. below). Ferguson, 15440a (ill-described); Wantrup, 259a. Estimate $600/900

description: THERRY, Sir Roger. REMINISCENCES OF THIRTY YEARS’ RESIDENCE in New South Wales and Victoria. With a supplementary chapter on transportation and the ticket-of-leave system. Octavo, title splitting at gutter, advertisement leaves foxed, uncut in modern green half crushed morocco, marbled boards. London, Sampson Low, Son, and Co., 1863. title: TWOPENY, Richard Ernest Nowell.
description: TWOPENY, Richard Ernest Nowell. TOWN LIFE IN AUSTRALIA. Octavo, original decorated cloth over bevelled boards, light marking, Wantrup copy with book label. London, Elliot Stock, 1883. First edition of this distinguished account of Australian city life in the prosperous decades following the gold rushes by the editor of the Pastoral Review. Town Life is “written in a crisp, lively style, with a touch of urbane irony. Twopeny’s interests are those of a considerably sophisticated (though less so than he thinks) man of the world... [He] excels in his observation of social life, perceiving for instance the “capitalist” temperament of Australians, the mobility of occupations, the hierarchy of the professions which was to become dominant for the next hundred odd years, the dominance of country “ideals” and the absence of a real town life and town “ideals”. In spite of his sharp tongue, he was fair-minded conceding that even the parvenu had the merit of seeking better things...” (Dorothy Green). Ferguson, 17433. Estimate $150/200

title: WENDEL, Robert. NEW SOUTH WALES ALBUM [cover title].
description: WENDEL, Robert. NEW SOUTH WALES ALBUM [cover title]. Oblong quarto, single leaf Preface and 22 unnumbered chromolithographs (two double-page) on 24 leaves, with printed text interleaves, the first plate with a small adhesion, several small splits at margins sealed, original half dark plum roan and plum cloth boards, title on the front board in gilt, neatly rebacked and with new endpapers. Sydney, Troedel& Co., 1878. Only edition. Charles Troedel established a Sydney branch following his considerable achievements in Melbourne. Aiming to repeat his success with the Melbourne Album a decade before, he commissioned a companion New South Wales Album. Rather than working with several contributors as he had with the Melbourne work, Troedel gave the task to Robert Wendel, whom Shuhkrafft had brought out to Melbourne with Troedel in 1860 and who had worked with Troedel on the Melbourne Album. Troedel issued the New South Wales Album in at least four – and probably more – different forms: this is the largest issue with the additional “History of New South Wales” including interleaved advertisements (one a chromolithograph) following the plates. The work is quite uncommon: due to adhesion of the chromolithographs in most copies, notorious in this book (and indeed in many books of the period using this colour process), only a limited number have survived undamaged. See Ferguson, 17332; Wantrup, 265. Estimate $1200/1800

title: WITHERS, William Bramwell.
description: WITHERS, William Bramwell. THE HISTORY OF BALLARAT, from the first pastoral settlement to the present time. Octavo, additional chromolithographed Eureka flag title-page, folding panorama, plates, a good copy in original cloth. Ballarat, “Ballarat Star”, 1870. First edition. Withers’s historical research was well-based on five years’ correspondence and interviews with pioneer diggers and squatters, and with eye-witnesses at Eureka. He produced a comprehensive and magisterial work, well-documented, fluently-written, and objective, a major achievement of nineteenth-century Australian historiography and a paradigm of Australian local history writing unsurpassed for decades. Above all, Withers’s perceptive and judicial interpretation of the Eureka Rebellion is one of the best accounts, marshalling and objectively evaluating an impressively detailed record of first-hand evidence. Withers’s History is also well illustrated with a large folding panoramic view of Ballarat, plates of views and facsimile documents as well as a fine additional title-leaf with a coloured representation of the famous “Southern Cross” Eureka flag of white cross and silver stars on a blue ground. Ferguson 18713. Estimate $400/600 Important Colonial Literature (lots 73 –111)

title: [WARING, Charlotte, Mrs James Atkinson, later Mrs George Barton].
description: [WARING, Charlotte, Mrs James Atkinson, later Mrs George Barton]. MOTHER’S OFFERING TO HER CHILDREN: By a Lady, Long Resident in New South Wales. Duodecimo, printing flaw on one leaf (pp. 181-2), slightly affecting imposition but not legibility, uncut in attractive recent half morocco by Sangorski & Sutcliffe. Sydney, Printed at the “Gazette” Office, [1841]. Rare. This first Australian book for children, published in Sydney in 1841, is uncompromisingly – and importantly so – Australian in content. The anonymous author is at pains to emphasise the truth of what she narrates and that “it may claim some trifling merit also from being the first work written in the Colony expressly for Children”. It is now known that the book was written by Charlotte Waring, one of the colony’s most remarkable women, whose married name at that point was Charlotte Barton. Charlotte Waring had come to Australia in 1826 as governess to the family of Hannibal Macarthur. She met James Atkinson, the agriculturist and author, on the voyage and they married. The Atkinsons had four children, one of whom was novelist and naturalist Louisa Atkinson. When James died in 1834, Charlotte Atkinson married George Barton, supervisor of the Atkinson property Oldbury in the Southern Highlands. Sadly, her second husband became insane and Charlotte Barton had to leave Oldbury and escape to Sydney with her children. Presenting a series of conversations between a mother and her children on a range of subjects, this carefully crafted book clearly benefited from Waring’s experience as a governess and skilfully demonstrates what was the predominant form of family education at the time. The topics of conversation are roughly divided between those relating to the natural history of the children’s Australian environment, terrifying tales of Australian shipwrecks, and accounts of distant settlements in the Australian north, all drawn from recent colonial history. The very detailed and circumstantial accounts of shipwrecks and northern settlement are used to educate her children about matters well beyond the shipwrecks themselves. As one of her children says, “We are very, very sorry for the poor people who suffer through them, Mamma; but it is very interesting to hear of so many things that occur in consequence, quite new to us, you know”. The remaining conversations relate to natural history. It is instructive to read these ‘lessons’ in light of what we know of the vital role played by women in promoting knowledge of the Australian environment. Significantly, Charlotte addresses these topics from an Australian point of view assuming, as a matter of course, that her children know only their own environment and not the alien British environment of squirrel, badger, and deer. When she does stray to foreign topics, as in “The Purple Beetle”, emphasis is laid on the alien nature of the subject – “something that you saw in England, if you please, Mamma: and then it will be quite new to us”. The lessons are often delightfully anecdotal. The lesson “Extraordinary Sounds” includes an account of an incident which Hamilton Hume had experienced when exploring with Charles Sturt related by him at Appin to a visiting “gentleman” – perhaps James Atkinson? The most anecdotal lesson is the final one, “Anecdotes of the Aborigines of New South Wales”. Much information on the customs and lives of the local Aborigines is shared as Charlotte recounts the unhappy tale of an Aboriginal woman, Nanny, and her baby daughter, Sally. The narrative has such a ring of truth that it must have been drawn from Charlotte’s personal experience in her contact with the Aboriginal tribes in the Southern Highlands. This is one of the most significant books published in the early decades of settlement, revealing as nowhere else the process of Australianisation of the native-born and the key role played in that process by the women of the family. A Mother’s Offering is a rare book of acknowledged importance. Ferhuson, 3185; Wantrup, 487. Estimate $15,000/30,000

title: BARTON, George Burnett.
description: BARTON, George Burnett. LITERATURE OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Octavo, modern half calf, Ingleton copy with bookplate. Sydney, Thomas Richards, 1866. First edition: “the first attempt to direct attention to the works of colonial writers” (Ferguson). Barton was the first to treat Australian literature with sustained critical standards that made no patronising allowance for the ‘infancy’ of colonial literature. With uncompromising standards based on the entire tradition of Western literature, Barton rarely gave praise but, when he did, his judgements have largely stood the test of time. + BARTON, George Burnett. THE POETS AND PROSE WRITERS OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Octavo, later half blue morocco. Sydney, Gibbs, Shallard, & Co., 1866. Estimate $200/400

title: BEDFORD, Ruth. RHYMES BY RUTH. Sextodecimo, pp.
description: BEDFORD, Ruth. RHYMES BY RUTH. Sextodecimo, pp. 32, original decorated wrappers (bit friable on spine). Petersham (Sydney), Frederick J. Ridley, 1896. Rare. The first booklet of verse published by Bedford, written between her fourteenth and eighteenth years. She subsequently pursued a career as a freelance writer, publishing several volumes of verse, fiction, children’s verse and stories, drama, as well as contributing regularly to magazines and journals here and overseas. She is often compared to Dorothea Mackellar, with whom she did, indeed, collaborate. Published by the author herself in 1893 and again in 1896, this first volume of rhymes is rare in either edition and one of few notable juvenile publications by subsequently successful Australian writers. Miller, 270; not included by Muir who is annoyingly inconsistent in such matters. Estimate $150/300

The first story, “The Mystery of Major Molineux”, is a psychological suspense thriller set in Tasmania, while “Human Repetends” is a similar tale set in Melbourne. Estimate $200/400

This Hobart issue is one of several concurrent issues with the imprints of M’Carron, Bird & Co (Melbourne), E.S. Wigg & Son (Adelaide), Watson, Ferguson & Co. (Brisbane), E.R. Cole (Sydney), and Walch Bros. (Hobart). Estimate $150/300

title: CLARKE, Marcus. HIS NATURAL LIFE Three volumes, octavo, original cloth, decorated and lettered in gilt and black, the cl
description: CLARKE, Marcus. HIS NATURAL LIFE Three volumes, octavo, original cloth, decorated and lettered in gilt and black, the cloth with signs of use, a very good copy. London, Richard Bentley and Son, 1875. Rare: the first London edition of Clarke’s epic historical novel of the convict system, one of the classic novels of the colonial era. Considered by many to be the greatest novel of the colonial era, it has effectively remained in print since its first publication and has been dramatised, filmed, televised, abridged, anthologised, and translated, playing a key role in the constructed romance of Australia’s past, a contribution as crucial as that made by Scott for European writing and by Cooper for American literature. His Natural Life was first printed as a serial in the Australian Journal between March 1870 and June 1872. This serial text was heavily edited for book publication in Melbourne in 1874, with substantial structural and thematic changes made. Indeed, so great were these changes, especially thematically, that one can say that the serial novel, with its positive view of human resilience, and the much more pessimistic book are actually two different works. Clarke acknowledged Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, with which His Natural Life shares a central moral concern, although Clarke’s pessimistic conclusion in the book edition is very different from Hugo’s. London bookseller Baillière, charged by George Robertson with finding the novel an English publisher, settled with Richard Bentley and Son. Unlike London editions of other Australian novels, Bentley’s edition is of greater importance in the book’s subsequent history than the edition published in Melbourne, which was never reprinted. Clarke’s text was extensively revised by Mrs Cashel Hoey for the London edition, with the guidance of Bentley’s famous readers Geraldine Jewsbury and Charlotte Jackson. It is this Bentley version that was reprinted in one volume in 1878 and many times reprinted until the end of the century – changing the title without permission to For the Term of His Natural Life in the 1882 impression, thereby erasing the implicit irony of Clarke’s original title on a work that detailed an overwhelmingly unnatural life. Macmillan, who bought Richard Bentley and Son in 1899, continued to reprint that version well into the 1930s. These new impressions of the one-volume edition account for tens of thousands of copies and it has been the familiar text of the novel for well over a century. It is still in print today in that form. Only 750 copies of the three-volume first Bentley edition were printed, 206 of which were remaindered as unbound sheets – probably to clear the decks for the more profitable one-volume edition of 1878. The Bentley edition is rarely seen and, from an historical perspective, is as highly valued as the Melbourne edition of 1874. Loder, p. 54; Miller, p. 611; Sadleir, 560a; Wantrup, 515c; Wolff, 1247 (but no copy). Estimate $2000/4000 Lot 81

title: DE BOOS, Charles. FIFTY YEARS AGO: AN AUSTRALIAN TALE. Octavo, in an attractive contemporary Sydney binding of half calf
description: DE BOOS, Charles. FIFTY YEARS AGO: AN AUSTRALIAN TALE. Octavo, in an attractive contemporary Sydney binding of half calf by Corbett with his ticket, some non-disturbing stains in the early margins, scattered foxing throughout (as usual), very good. Sydney, Gordon and Gotch, 1867. First and only edition: an author’s copy of this rare and important novel – the first Australian historical novel and one addressed to an exclusively Australian audience, and the first to deal powerfully with the problem of relations between Aborigines and settlers. Charles De Boos, a highly respected journalist, was best known to contemporaries as the Parliamentary reporter for the Sydney Morning Herald (the basic premise of the plot of his novel was inspired by the case of the murderer Joseph Wilkes, exposed by the investigations of a Parliamentary committee in 1857). Today Fifty Years Ago is effectively unknown to general readers and has only recently been embraced by academic critics. First brought to notice by Clive Hamer and J. J. Healy over fifty years ago(!) and more recently championed by Victor Crittenden, who also reprinted it, it is only in the last two decades that this severely underrated novel has been given due attention. It is one of the major literary achievements of the colonial period. The action of Fifty Years Ago is dramatic but it is not sensationalised; it is as much a novel of moral and societal contemplation as it is one of action. Set in the lower Hunter Valley in the time of Governor Macquarie, the novel opens with the massacre of the family of a settler, George Maxwell, by Aborigines of the Maroo tribe, followed by the vengeance exacted by him over many years as he tracks down and kills the leaders, accompanied by his increasingly deranged young son, Jamie. Having exterminated the tribe, assisted by a young Aboriginal woman, Eumerella, who also wanted revenge for her abduction and rape, Maxwell now sets his sights on the last of the tribe, the chief Macomo. Eventually, however, Maxwell grows into a new understanding of the Aborigines and comes to respect Macomo, who by his later actions has grown in our estimation also. “The novel successfully captures both the physical environment and the psychological ambience of those colonial times; its somewhat revolutionary conclusion in favour of the Aborigines contrasts greatly, however, with the disparagement of them so widely aired in other colonial literature” (OCAL). The present copy is an author’s copy, with his ownership signature on the first four leaves. It was then in the collection of James H. Rainford, actor, theatrical manager, politician, and publican. Rainford has cheekily added his small discrete ownership stamp to the dedication page to give the impression that the book was dedicated to him as well as to John Fairfax – almost certainly a private joke between him and the author, both of whom moved in the same social circles and were probably more than just acquaintances. Miller p. 608; Wantrup, 514. Estimate $1000/2000

description: FOX, Lady Mary, and others. ACCOUNT OF AN EXPEDITION to the Interior of New Holland. Edited by Lady Mary Fox. Duodecimo, without the half-title, modern half calf and marbled boards. London, Richard Bentley, 1837. First edition. A bizarre tale of an exploring expedition which set out from Bathurst in 1835 to penetrate further into the interior of New South Wales, where the explorers encounter a group of English-speaking native inhabitants. Ferguson, 2264. Estimate $300/500

title: FURPHY, Joseph. SUCH IS LIFE. Being Certain Extracts From the Diary of Tom Collins.
description: FURPHY, Joseph. SUCH IS LIFE. Being Certain Extracts From the Diary of Tom Collins. Octavo, original decorated cloth little flecked, old news-clipping on the advertisement leaf with consequent offsetting. Sydney, The Bulletin Newspaper Company, 1903. The extremely scarce first edition of a classic first book and one of the most important works of the Nationalist period of Australian literature. Championed by many critics and authors over the decades, Furphy’s picaresque depiction of Australian life in the backblocks has come to hold the highest reputation, some even labelling it ‘the great Australian novel’. Furphy and his contemporary, Henry Lawson, are regarded as the pre-eminent exponents of the bush theme in Australian fiction. Furphy began this novel in 1893 and it was finally published by the Bulletin in 1903. It met with a mediocre critical reception and moderate sales and in 1917 the 800 remaining copies were bought up and reissued by Kate Baker with a new title-page and an introduction by Vance Palmer. This second issue is comparatively common, whereas the first edition is now an extremely scarce book indeed. Mackaness and Stone, XXX; Miller, p. 689. Estimate $200/400

title: HARRIS, Alexander. THE EMIGRANT FAMILY: or, The Story of an Australian Settler.
description: HARRIS, Alexander. THE EMIGRANT FAMILY: or, The Story of an Australian Settler. By the Author of “Settlers and Convicts”. Three volumes, octavo, uncut in original cloth-backed boards with paper spine labels, neat owner’s inscription dated 1849 on the endpapers, a very good set with expected signs of use and age (some insect damage to the cloth on the spines, labels slightly chipped, endpapers foxed and with paste residue from old protective cloth sleeves since removed, some non-disturbing damp marks at the back of two volumes). London, Smith, Elder and Co., 1849. First edition of a very rare and important three-decker novel. Dorothy Green, among others, speaks highly of “the immensely civilized, rational and humane temper of this first genuinely Australian novel”. A ‘black sheep’ smuggled by his family to New South Wales in 1825, Alexander Harris continued at first to lead the rather low life that he had followed in London and worked at different times as a clerk and tutor, as a cedar-getter and rural worker, working and travelling in the regions around the Hunter Valley, the Illawarra, and the Shoalhaven until leaving Australia in 1840 after sixteen years. Returning to London he became associated with the movement to promote emigration and wrote or co-wrote several works, most notably his classic account of Australian backwoods life, Settlers and Convicts; or Recollections of Sixteen Years’ Labour in the Australian Backwoods by an Emigrant Mechanic, the most significant early articulation of the spirit of Australian egalitarianism. Harris’s sympathies were always with the native-born and the emancipists rather than with the official class and his books are essentially a fictionalised presentation of his own experiences. Writing with true literary flair and an infallible gift for articulating the distinctive qualities of life as he experienced it around him, Harris gives in that and his other books the most realistic and comprehensive account of early Australian life we have. It must also be said that Harris was also a most perceptive recorder of the Australian dialect and he often provides the earliest, or most illuminating, citation of Australianisms which were to become the currency of Australian speech over the next century and a half. His only work of fiction, The Emigrant Family: or, The Story of an Australian Settler, published anonymously, was written within the conventions of the emigrant novel. In it Harris focuses on the realities of the colonial society in which he had been an engaged participant, and on the nascent distinctive attitudes of the ordinary Australian settler. His affectionately depicted settings are conspicuously real and not contrived backgrounds for melodramatic adventure. Indeed, it is his ability to depict a rounded view of society and of nature in Australia that separates The Emigrant Family from preceding Australian novels, making this not only the major novel of the period but the first genuinely Australian novel. When a new cheap edition of the novel was published in 1852 by Routledge in their Railway Library series, retitled Martin Beck: or, the Story of An Australian Settler, Alexander Harris was finally acknowledged as the author. Ferguson, 5061; Miller, p. 597; not in Sadleir; Wantrup, 492; not in Wolff (but see 3014 for 1850 second issue). Estimate $2000/4000 Lot 87

title: HEALEY, Daniel. THE SEVEN CHRISTIANS OF CHAMPIONDOM. A Tale of the Times.
description: HEALEY, Daniel. THE SEVEN CHRISTIANS OF CHAMPIONDOM. A Tale of the Times. Quarto, original half cloth and marbled boards, gilt title-label on the front board, the binding a little used, very good, copy of John Lane Mullins with Sancta Sophia bookplate. Written and published for and by The Author. Sydney, N.S.W. Australia, 1885. Very rare nineteenth–century dystopian satirical novel, set in a thinly disguised ‘Yednis’. Healy is best known for his volume of satirical verse, The Cornstalk: His Habits and Habitat (Sydney, 1893), but this piece is virtually unrecorded. The title is a subversion on a very popular and often reprinted 1597 book by Richard Johnson, The Seven Champions of Christendom, a collection of mythical and semi-mythical biographies of European saints. Aficionados of Mr Ponzi will recognise at the heart of the satire an elaborate proto-Ponzi scheme involving property – not surprising, it is Sydney. The novel is printed by a form of lithographic process reproducing manuscript – the bestknown example of this process is William Bland’s 1892 Account of the Duel between William Bland & Robert Case. The advantage of this style of printing may be that it allowed for printing and reprinting small numbers of copies at a time, a proceeding that would be prohibitive with letterpress. title: LAWSON, Henry. SHORT STORIES IN PROSE AND VERSE. Octavo, wood-block illustrations and decorations throughout (some full-
description: LAWSON, Henry. SHORT STORIES IN PROSE AND VERSE. Octavo, wood-block illustrations and decorations throughout (some full-page and some by B.E. Minns), bound with the original wrappers in a handsome signed binding by the celebrated Wal Taylor, full morocco, gilt and decorated, edges gilt. Sydney, Louisa Lawson, 1894. An attractively presented copy of the first and only edition of the first book by a great Australian writer, printed and published by his mother, an outstanding early Australian feminist who employed only women for her printing and publishing ventures. The volume was itself a nationalistic statement: “an attempt to publish, in Australia, a collection of sketches and stories at a time when everything Australian... must bear the imprint of a London publishing firm before our critics will condescend to notice it”. But in the end Lawson was unhappy with the book and his inscription in David Scott Mitchell’s copy reads: “This is my first book. Only a few copies were published fortunately. I withdrew the book from publication. The book should be interesting as a curiosity in printing”. Despite this self-deprecating tone, some of Lawson’s best-known and most enduring work was printed here, including “The Drover’s Wife” and “The Union Buries its Dead”. title: PEDLEY, Ethel C. DOT AND THE KANGAROO. Octavo, black & white plates by Frank Mahony, original red cloth in custom made box with leather label.
description: PEDLEY, Ethel C. DOT AND THE KANGAROO. Octavo, black & white plates by Frank Mahony, original red cloth in custom made box with leather label. London, Thomas Burleigh, 1899. The rare first edition of this Australian children’s classic. A “fundamental text of Australian children’s literature” (Richards), Pedley’s tale of a little girl lost in the bush who is helped by a kindly grey kangaroo has hardly been out of print since it was first published. Illustrated by numerous artists over the years, this first edition is the only contemporary edition with the full suite of Bulletin artist Frank Mahony’s classic and authentically Australian illustrations. Angus and Robertson acquired the rights to the book after its first publication but did not reproduce all these illustrations until their much later edition of 1920. Although Pedley died in England shortly before the book was published, she had arranged beforehand for Mahony to illustrate the book and, as the publisher states in an introductory note, “this book, though printed and published in England, was entirely produced in Australia. The writer – now no more – was deeply attached to the land of her adoption, and it was by her special arrangement that the illustrations were drawn by Mr. Frank Mahony, and the plates etched by Messrs. Benton and Bacon, of Sydney”. Estimate $400/600

title: PORTER, Sarah Ricardo, Mrs G.R. ALFRED DUDLEY; or, The Australian Settlers.
description: PORTER, Sarah Ricardo, Mrs G.R. ALFRED DUDLEY; or, The Australian Settlers. Duodecimo, frontispiece and three other engraved plates, uncut in the original bind-stamped cloth, spine lettered and decorated in gilt, rebacked preserving the original spine and endpapers. London, Printed for Harvey and Darton, 1830. First edition and extremely scarce: the first work of children’s fiction set entirely in Australia. The plot is “founded on the circumstances of a gentleman, with his highly educated son, settling in Australia and there for a long period cheerfully submitting to all the hardships and privations attendant on such a situation” (Ferguson). The book also includes a short glossary of the “Australian” (i.e. Aboriginal) language. Ferguson, 1313 (miscollated); Muir, 6077 (not in original binding and bound without advertisements). title: ROWCROFT, Charles. THE BUSHRANGER, of Van Diemen’s Land.
description: ROWCROFT, Charles. THE BUSHRANGER, of Van Diemen’s Land. Three volumes, 12mo, entirely uncut in publisher’s original plum rib-grain cloth-backed boards, printed paper spine labels (bit distressed), very neatly recased with new endpapers. London, Smith Elder and Co., 1846. First edition: author’s inscribed presentation copy of one of the earliest Australian novels. The Bushranger of Van Diemen’s Land was designed as a continuation of Rowcroft’s very popular and many times reprinted Tales of the Colonies, with the half-title of the first volume and the three spine labels headed “Second Series of Tales of the Colonies”. In his second novel Rowcroft accentuated and extended the melodramatic and sensational element at the expense of the balanced didacticism of his first novel. In The Bushrangers the settler’s experience is set from the beginning within a sensational world of violent convicts and bushrangers, both white and black, including the notorious black convict Mosquito, a white woman captive of the Aborigines, and so on. The novel did not enjoy the same success as Tales of the Colonies and sold slowly, remaining in print for a long time. There was no second edition. Whether he intended to or not, Rowcroft set the pattern for Australian fiction within the emigrant novel sub-genre for some time. The settler facing the perils presented by nature and man and the satisfaction that comes from surmounting them remained a constant in popular Australian fiction. The emphasis on the exotic, on the ‘otherness’ of Australia, appealed to the British public and this fascination with the ‘other’ can even be seen persisting in the Bulletin writers of the 1890s who emphasised the exotic ‘other’ world of the bush for the benefit of the local urban population whom they largely addressed. Ferguson, 4374; Miller, 596; not in Sadleir; Wantrup, 489; Wolff, 5977. Estimate $600/900

No author’s name was given to this contribution and the first edition in book form which acknowledged Sargent as the author did not appear until eleven years later. title: TURNER, Ethel. SEVEN LITTLE AUSTRALIANS. Octavo, three plates, few ownership marks, illustrations throughout, diffuse fo
description: TURNER, Ethel. SEVEN LITTLE AUSTRALIANS. Octavo, three plates, few ownership marks, illustrations throughout, diffuse foxing, original gilt-decorated pictorial russet cloth bit shaken and used but a decent copy. London, Ward, Lock & Bowden, 1894. Rare: the first edition of Ethel Turner’s classic first book, translated into at least eight languages and reprinted in English so often that there is no authoritative count of the editions. Turner was very conscious of the quite revolutionary nature of her novel, as one can see from her introductory remarks. This was the first Australian children’s book to present children realistically, with both good and bad behaviours and characteristics, rather than as the idealised pious prigs hitherto commonly presented in English children’s literature. The novel was an important expression of the nationalist sentiment of the times and, in many respects, one of the single most significant expressions of it. Turner was quite deliberate in stating that it was the ‘Australianness’ of her characters, both child and adult, that determined her to adopt this revolutionary style of characterisation. Her treatment, for example, of Meg’s unsuccessful adventure in flirtation at sixteen is quite remarkable both for the, at the time, uncommonly daring plot that has an adolescent girl arranging to meet a young man some years her senior secretly and late in the evening, and for the truthfulness of Turner’s presentation of Meg’s inner turmoil. It was this ‘bold and free’ but engagingly unaffected nature of Australian young women that was remarked upon by visitors from the earliest years of the colony well into the twentieth century. Seven Little Australians also brought about a revolution in Australian reading habits. Before the publication of this novel, few if any such stories for young people were published for an Australian audience. Australian-produced children’s books were largely ephemeral or didactic publications and for children’s fiction the Australian market was satisfied by the British publications of British authors – with a few Americans thrown in. Recreational reading for the Australian child was entirely an imported product. Although published in England, this novel marked the single most radical change in the reading habits of young Australians and consequently in the practice of Australian writing and publishing for children. Michael Richards described Seven Little Australians as ‘the book at the heart of the 1890s’. Brenda Niall characterised the whole decade as Ethel Turner’s: “this was the decade of little pickles, little rebels, little larrikins and – instead of young Anglo-Australians – little Australians”. Miller, p. 663; People, Print & Paper, 201; Wantrup, 522a. Estimate $800/1200

title: WENTWORTH, William Charles.
description: WENTWORTH, William Charles. AUSTRALASIA. A POEM. Written for the Chancellor’s Medal at the Cambridge Commencement, July, 1823. Octavo, bound in more recent half morocco over marbled boards, the binder’s blanks and endpapers spotted but an attractive copy. London, G. and W.B. Whittacker, 1823. The rare first edition of the first volume of verse published by an Australian-born poet and the second published volume of Australian verse, preceded only by English-born Barron Field’s fabulously rare 1819 First Fruits of Australian Poetry. Wentworth, explorer, orator, historian and later to be one of Australia’s leading statesmen, founding a political dynasty which extended well into the twentieth century, While the poem is stylistically imitative of the English Augustan poets, it has always had special appeal to Australians and the colonial public was most familiar with the last dozen, Union-Jack-waving, lines. To us, probably the most moving portion of this long poem is explorer Wentworth’s description of his own feelings upon crossing the Blue Mountains as he saw: The boundless champaign burst upon our sight, Till, nearer seen, the beauteous landscape grew, Op’ning like Canaan on rapt Israel’s view. Wentworth’s poem won second place in the Cambridge competition, the first prize went to the often patently absurd poem of an English undergraduate, W.M. Praed, a competent versifier who had never set foot in Australia (although he had been to Eton, of course). Forty years later G.B. Barton commented, mildly enough, that “a comparison of the two productions will suggest doubts to some readers as to the justice of the award”. title: AMUNDSEN, Roald. THE SOUTH POLE: an Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the “Fram”, 1910 – 1912. Two volume
description: AMUNDSEN, Roald. THE SOUTH POLE: an Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the “Fram”, 1910 – 1912. Two volumes, thick octavo, with all maps and plates, an impressively clean set in the original decorated red buckram, spotted fore-edge foxing, top edges gilt, others uncut, a couple of corners bruised, spine flags little dulled as always. The commander’s narrative of this most important expedition, the first attainment of the South Pole in competition with Captain Robert Falcon Scott. Racing against Scott’s party, Amundsen and his party reached the Pole in December 1911, some 34 days before Scott. “Amundsen’s modest account of his extraordinary South Pole exploit is a classic in the exploration literature” (Rosove). This was the only substantial contemporary account of the expedition. Renard, 17; Rosove, 9.A1; Spence, 16. Estimate $1000/1500

title: BORCHGREVINK, Carsten E. FIRST ON THE ANTARCTIC CONTINENT: being an Account of the British Antarctic Expedition, 1898 –
description: BORCHGREVINK, Carsten E. FIRST ON THE ANTARCTIC CONTINENT: being an Account of the British Antarctic Expedition, 1898 – 1900. Octavo, with photogravure frontispiece portrait, three folding tinted maps, numerous illustrations in the text (many full-page), and pp. 32 (advertisements dated in code “1.01” on the first page), original silver and gilt pictorial cloth, fine, spine gilt faded, front board lettered in gilt and with an attractive gilt and silver block of a ship in ice, top edge gilt, others uncut. London, Newnes, 1901. First edition (primary binding) of an attractive and important book. This is the leader and organiser’s account of the Antarctic cruise of the Southern Cross, the first expedition to winter in the Antarctic continent and the first to use dogs in the Antarctic. The party made first landings on Coulman Island and Ross Island, built a hut at Cape Adare, and were the first to travel over the Ross Ice Shelf, establishing a new furthest south. title: DAVIS, John King. WITH THE “AURORA” IN THE ANTARCTIC 1911 – 1914. Quarto, plates, maps and illustrations, a coupleof pag
description: DAVIS, John King. WITH THE “AURORA” IN THE ANTARCTIC 1911 – 1914. Quarto, plates, maps and illustrations, a coupleof pages marked from loosely inserted bookmark, faint date stamps on rear endpaper, original dark blue buckram (spine gilt dulled as often), the boards marked, gilt vignette on front board. Davis was also commander of the Nimrod during Shackleton’s 1907-9 expedition as well as commander of the 1916 Ross Sea Relief Expedition. title: MAWSON, Douglas. THE HOME OF THE BLIZZARD: BEING THE STORY OF THE AUSTRALASIAN ANTARCTIC EXPEDITION 1911 – 1914. Two vol
description: MAWSON, Douglas. THE HOME OF THE BLIZZARD: BEING THE STORY OF THE AUSTRALASIAN ANTARCTIC EXPEDITION 1911 – 1914. Two volumes, thick octavo, with in total 196 leaves of monochrome plates (including photogravure frontispieces with titling-tissue), seven double-page plates, and two folding plates, eighteen leaves of coloured plates with titling-tissues, three large folding tinted end-pocket maps, other illustrations (including maps) in the text; original silver-pictorial dark blue rib-grain cloth, joints rubbed at foot of spine in first volume, spines lettered and ruled in gilt, front boards lettered in gilt with a central vignette in silver, titled in the image “Leaning on the Wind”, back boards with publisher’s device in blind; bottom edges uncut; a particularly fine set, inscribed by the author. London, William Heinemann, 1915. First edition. with Mawson’s signed inscription in both volumes, 1916, to Professor Archibald Watson, celebrated Adelaide academic and surgeon. An uncommonly bright set of the classic account of Australian Antarctic exploration, frequently reprinted, revised, abridged, and translated. Mawson’s first expedition was an epic of endurance and this and his subsequent work in the Antarctic form the most significant basis to Australia’s claim to its extensive Antarctic Territory. The expedition charted the entire coastline between the Mertz Glacier and Grassberg, forming the last link in the chain that connected the discoveries of Dumont d’Urville, Wilkes, Scott, and Drygalski. Most importantly, they systematically explored King George V Land and the adjacent Terra Adelie. Mawson’s book includes a self-effacing account of his epic journey across five hundred kilometres of Adelie Land in 1912, without a tent and most of his food, “one of the great feats of human endurance” (Richards). title: SCOTT, Captain Robert F. THE VOYAGE OF THE ‘DISCOVERY’. Two volumes, thick octavo, plates, coloured plates (from waterco

A collection of short fiction, published by the author himself in a limited edition, numbered and signed. The limitation is unstated but copies are known numbered as high as 193 and a limitation of 200-250 is almost certain. Porter undertook publication himself because he found Australian publishers were not prepared to accept any fiction with an urban or suburban locale, preferring fiction based on rural experience. The rarity of the book has been credited to the author’s eccentrically bibulous method of distribution. description: SLESSOR, Kenneth. THIEF OF THE MOON. Kirtley, 1924. Rare: Slessor’s first published work with a suite of Norman Lindsay’s engravings. Number 72 of an edition purporting to be limited to 130 copies signed by the author. Although all proposed copies of the text were actually printed and bound, John Kirtley has several times recorded that at least half the edition was destroyed by a fire in the warehouse where the bound copies were stored. A similar reduction was suffered to the edition of Jack Lindsay’s Fauns and Ladies but a more substantial number of copies of Lindsay’s book had been distributed before the blaze. Of the surviving copies not many seem to have been distributed after the fire because Lindsay and Kirtley packed up and left for England soon after, taking with them the remaining bound copies. These bound copies were technically incomplete because, while Norman Lindsay had produced the requisite number of signed and numbered woodengravings, these had not all been tipped into their respective volumes. That chore was left until copies were actually despatched to buyers (the same was true of Fauns and Ladies). Accordingly, a substantial number of the 60 or 70 copies extant were never finished and never properly issued. Thief of the Moon, complete with the Norman Lindsay wood-engravings, is one of the more manifestly rare ‘first books’ by a major Australian writer. Arnold, The Fanfrolico Press (2009), 2 (suggesting that perhaps only a third of the edition was made up); Miller, p. 334; People, Print & Paper, 179; Serle, p. 184. Estimate $2000/4000
